title: A New Peace Deal for Israel and Lebanon—But One Big Group Says No
summary: Have you ever made a deal that someone else refused to follow? That’s what happened this week between Israel, Lebanon, and the United States. They signed a framework agreement—a kind of plan—to stop the fighting between Israel and a powerful armed group in Lebanon called Hezbollah. But Hezbollah immediately said, “No way!” The deal was announced on Friday after talks in Washington, D.C. It says the Lebanese army will take control of all Lebanese land, but only after Hezbollah gives up its weapons. Once that’s verified, Israeli soldiers can slowly pull out of southern Lebanon, where they’ve been since March. That’s when Israel launched a new offensive that has killed more than 4,000 people. Hezbollah’s leader, Naim Qassem, called the agreement “null and void”—meaning worthless. He insists that any peace must be based on a separate deal between Iran and the U.S. He also warned that linking Israel’s withdrawal to Hezbollah’s disarmament crosses “all red lines.” In Israel, reactions are mixed. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says the deal is a big blow to Iran and promises to keep a buffer zone until Hezbollah is disarmed. But opposition leader Yair Lapid worries Iran can still send money to Hezbollah. A local leader near the border, David Azoulay, is cautiously hopeful but says any Israeli withdrawal must be careful. So, will this plan actually work? As one expert said, “Only time and its implementation will determine.” That means we’ll have to wait and see.
why_it_matters: This shows how difficult peace can be when one powerful group says 'no'—much like when not everyone in your class agrees on the rules, making it hard to move forward.

background_read: Israel and Lebanon share a border and have been in conflict for decades, especially with Hezbollah, a heavily armed group based in Lebanon.
Hezbollah is supported by Iran, a country that often sees Israel as a rival.
The United States frequently steps in to help negotiate peace deals in the Middle East, though not all groups agree to follow them.
